details:
**The Wind-Up Bird Chronicle**
Murakami's sprawling 1994–95 novel, the most common title clue for him. It opens with the unemployed Toru Okada searching for his missing cat at the request of his wife Kumiko, who soon disappears as well; the cat is named Noboru Wataya after Kumiko's sinister politician brother.

**Norwegian Wood**
Murakami's 1987 breakthrough bestseller, named after the Beatles song. It opens with Toru Watanabe on a plane landing in Hamburg, where hearing a cover of the song makes him remember his college years in 1960s Tokyo.

**Toru Watanabe, Naoko, and Midori**
The love triangle at the center of Norwegian Wood. The fragile Naoko, whose boyfriend Kizuki (Toru's best friend) killed himself, withdraws to a sanatorium in the mountains where Toru visits her, while the outgoing Midori offers Toru a different life; Naoko eventually commits suicide as well.

**1Q84**
Murakami's longest novel (2009–10), whose title puns on George Orwell's 1984, since the Japanese word for nine ("kyu") sounds like the letter Q. Its two protagonists, Aomame and Tengo, find themselves in an alternate 1984 Tokyo with two moons in the sky, and the book ends with the two of them leaving that world together.

**Janáček's Sinfonietta**
The piece of music playing on the radio of a taxi stuck in traffic at the opening of 1Q84. Aomame then climbs out of the taxi and down an emergency stairway off the expressway, entering the alternate reality.

**Air Chrysalis and the Little People**
Air Chrysalis is a novel within 1Q84, told by the dyslexic teenager Fuka-Eri and rewritten by the math teacher and aspiring writer Tengo. It describes the supernatural "Little People." Fuka-Eri's father is the Leader of the religious cult Sakigake, which grew out of the Takashima commune; Aomame is sent to kill the Leader by the Dowager.

**Kafka on the Shore**
Murakami's 2002 novel whose odd and even chapters follow two storylines. The odd chapters follow a fifteen-year-old runaway who renames himself Kafka after Franz Kafka, has an alter ego called "the boy named Crow," and hides in Miss Saeki's library with the help of Oshima. The even chapters follow Nakata, an elderly, mentally impaired man who can talk to cats.

**Johnnie Walker**
The cat-killer in Kafka on the Shore who takes the form of the whisky-label figure and kills cats to make a flute out of their souls. Nakata kills him, after which fish rain from the sky. Another abstract figure, appearing as Colonel Sanders, helps the truck driver Hoshino find the "entrance stone."

**The Thieving Magpie**
The Rossini overture the narrator listens to while cooking spaghetti at the opening of The Wind-Up Bird Chronicle; he remarks that its length is the perfect time to cook pasta. "The Thieving Magpie" is also the title of the novel's first part, and the opening chapter first appeared as a story in The Elephant Vanishes.

**Lieutenant Mamiya and the well**
In The Wind-Up Bird Chronicle, the veteran Lieutenant Mamiya tells Toru of his service in Manchukuo, of watching a fellow officer skinned alive by "Boris the Manskinner," and of his time at the bottom of a dry well. Toru himself later sits at the bottom of a dry well and comes out with a blue-black mark on his cheek.

**May Kasahara, Malta and Creta Kano, Nutmeg and Cinnamon**
Supporting characters in The Wind-Up Bird Chronicle. May Kasahara is a morbid teenage girl who writes letters to Toru; the clairvoyant sisters Malta and Creta Kano help in the search, with Creta calling herself a "prostitute of the mind"; Nutmeg is drawn to Toru's mark, and her mute son Cinnamon keeps a secret computer archive titled "The Wind-Up Bird Chronicle."

**Trilogy of the Rat and Hear the Wind Sing**
Murakami's early sequence: Hear the Wind Sing (1979), his first novel, in which the narrator spends a summer drinking with his friend "the Rat" at J's Bar and meets a nine-fingered girl; Pinball, 1973, involving a translator's hunt for a three-flipper "Spaceship" pinball machine; and A Wild Sheep Chase. Murakami said he decided to write Hear the Wind Sing while watching Dave Hilton hit a double at a baseball game, and the first novel features the invented writer Derek Hartfield. The first two were republished in English as Wind/Pinball in 2015.

**A Wild Sheep Chase**
The 1982 novel concluding the Trilogy of the Rat proper (Dance Dance Dance is a later sequel). After the narrator publishes a pastoral photograph sent by the Rat, the right-hand man of "the Boss," a dying man with a blood cyst in his brain, forces him to find a sheep with a star-shaped mark on its back. His girlfriend with extraordinary ears leads him to the Dolphin Hotel and the Sheep Professor, and the search ends near the Hokkaido town of Junitaki.

**Hard-Boiled Wonderland and the End of the World**
A 1985 novel alternating between two worlds. In "Hard-Boiled Wonderland," a "Calcutec" who uses his brain to encrypt data is threatened by data-stealing "Semiotecs" and dates a very hungry librarian. In "The End of the World," a man reads old dreams from unicorn skulls in a walled town where people lose their minds once their shadows die.

**After Dark, Sputnik Sweetheart, and Killing Commendatore**
Other Murakami novels used as clues. After Dark opens at a Denny's where Mari is reading and involves the beating of a Chinese prostitute at a love hotel. Sputnik Sweetheart is narrated by the schoolteacher "K," whose beloved Sumire disappears on a Greek island. Killing Commendatore follows a painter who searches for the missing girl Mariye. His short stories include "On Seeing the 100% Perfect Girl One Beautiful April Morning."
